guide.title: Getting a number back
guide.subtitle: Opt-out and opt-in are two directions of the same record
guide.excerpt: A recipient who opted out can opt back in. The platform deactivates the suppression record rather than deleting it, so the consent trail survives.

sections.h: The reverse action exists on purpose
p: Replying START, YES or UNSTOP removes the number from the active suppression set and sends a confirmation. Without this, a single STOP would be permanent with no path back — which is why opt-out and opt-in are required to be symmetric in the first place.
The command is matched as a whole message, not as a substring, so a message that merely contains the word does not trigger it.

Resubscribing clears the active state and records when and by whom it was done. The original opt-out stays in the record. That is what makes the consent trail auditable: you can answer "was this person suppressed on the day we sent to them?" long after the fact.
The same capability exists in the console, where a manual release is attributed to the operator who performed it.

Releasing a number affects the messages we send. It does not affect a block applied on the carrier side — with toll-free numbers in particular, the number may have been blocked upstream, and the recipient has to release that themselves. A record that reads "active" is not proof that the handset will accept a message.
sections.scope: Suppression and resubscription are implemented for the SMS channel.
